problem.text: Mary chose an even $4$-digit number $n$. She wrote down all the divisors of $n$ in increasing order from left to right: $1, 2, \ldots, \frac{n}{2}, n$. At some moment Mary wrote $323$ as a divisor of $n$. What is the smallest possible value of the next divisor written to the right of $323$?

steps.title: Where to start: factor $323$ and remember $n$ is small
steps.body: The clue is the size limit: $n$ has only $4$ digits, so $n\le 9999$, and $323$ is already a big divisor. Factor it first, because any number that divides $n$ brings all its prime factors along. Then ask what the next divisor $d$ can be without forcing $n$ past $9999$.

steps.title: The next divisor must share a factor with $323$
steps.body: Suppose the next divisor $d$ shared no prime factor with $323$. If two numbers with no common factor both divide $n$, then their product divides $n$ too. So $n$ would be a multiple of $323\cdot d$, and $d\ge 324$. Careful: this is why guesses like $324$ or $330$ fail, even though they are just above $323$.

your_turn.prompt: Why is $323\cdot 324$ impossible as a factor of $n$?
your_turn.answer: $323\cdot324$ is about $100{,}000$, far more than $9999$, so $n$ would have at least $5$ digits.

steps.title: List the candidates
steps.body: So $d$ is a multiple of $17$ or a multiple of $19$, and $d>323$. Since $323=17\cdot19$, the next multiples come from bumping one of the two factors up by $1$. The smallest candidate is the answer, as long as some even $4$-digit $n$ really works with it.

your_turn.prompt: What is the smallest multiple of $19$ that is bigger than $323$?

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: The smallest multiple of $17$ above $323$ is $17\cdot20=340$, which beats $342$. It works: take $n=2^2\cdot5\cdot17\cdot19=6460$, an even $4$-digit number with $323$ and $340$ as divisors. Divisors come in pairs $k$ and $\frac{6460}{k}$, so a divisor strictly between $323$ and $340$ would pair with one strictly between $\frac{6460}{340}=19$ and $\frac{6460}{323}=20$, and there is no integer there. The answer is **(C)**.

wrong_choices.A: $324$ is just the next number, but it shares no factor with $323=17\cdot19$, so $n$ would have to be a multiple of $323\cdot324$, which has too many digits.
wrong_choices.B: $330=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot11$ shares no factor with $323$, so $n$ would have to be a multiple of $323\cdot330$, far above $9999$.
wrong_choices.E: $646=2\cdot323$ comes from assuming the next divisor must be a multiple of $323$ itself. It only needs to share one factor, $17$ or $19$, with $323$.
